slides.title: 12.2.1 Adding and Removing Elements
keyPoints: std::vector owns a contiguous sequence whose logical size can change.
push_back appends an element, emplace_back constructs one from arguments, and pop_back removes the final element.
Erasing in the middle shifts later elements and has iterator-invalidation consequences.
Do not retain references to elements across arbitrary structural changes.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 12, use 12.2.1 Adding and Removing Elements as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. std::vector owns a contiguous sequence whose logical size can change. push_back appends an element, emplace_back constructs one from arguments, and pop_back removes the final element when the vector is nonempty. Erasing in the middle shifts later elements and has iterator-invalidation consequences. Do not retain references to elements across arbitrary structural changes. Reallocation can move every element to new storage, and erasure can invalidate positions at or after the removed element. Use indices or stable identifiers when the collection’s structure may change, and still validate those indices before use. A vector’s ownership simplifies allocation, but it does not make every borrowed access permanent. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 12.2.2 Understanding Size and Capacity
keyPoints: Size is the number of constructed elements available to the program.
Capacity is the amount of element storage available before another reallocation is required.
reserve(100) may provide capacity for at least 100 elements without creating them; accessing element 99 is still.
resize(100) changes the number of elements and initializes new ones as specified.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 12, use 12.2.2 Understanding Size and Capacity as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Size is the number of constructed elements available to the program. Capacity is the amount of element storage available before another reallocation is required. reserve(100) may provide capacity for at least 100 elements without creating them; accessing element 99 is still invalid until the size includes it. resize(100) changes the number of elements and initializes new ones as specified. Capacity growth is an implementation strategy, not an exact doubling promise. Repeated appends have amortized constant complexity under the container’s contract, while an individual growth can move many elements. Reserve when a credible upper estimate is known, but do not call reserve before every append in a way that defeats geometric growth. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 12.3.1 Comparing Fixed and Dynamic Storage
keyPoints: A fixed-size container makes the extent a compile-time property and avoids a separate resizing policy.
A vector accepts a runtime size and owns dynamic storage.
Both provide contiguous elements suitable for cache-friendly traversal and many library interfaces.
Consider total object size, maximum input size, copying behavior, and ownership.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 12, use 12.3.1 Comparing Fixed and Dynamic Storage as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A fixed-size container makes the extent a compile-time property and avoids a separate resizing policy. A vector accepts a runtime size and owns dynamic storage. Both provide contiguous elements suitable for cache-friendly traversal and many library interfaces. Consider total object size, maximum input size, copying behavior, and ownership. A huge local fixed array may exceed a platform’s practical stack budget, while an unnecessarily dynamic tiny object can add allocation overhead. These are workload and platform questions. Avoid memorizing “array is fast, vector is slow” as a design rule; equivalent element loops can have very similar generated code when the surrounding storage policy is appropriate. slides.title: Append only inside a logical size limit
keyPoints: Append value only when it is -100 through 100 and size is below limit. Otherwise return false unchanged. limit is at most 100. Allocation failures may propagate; they are not represented by false.
